claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys is governed by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys is governed by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces relieve local stress concentrations associated with premature crack initiation.
Stress-concentration relief by coherent nanoprecipitates delays crack initiation under high-temperature loading.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous matrix with minimal pre-existing controlled nanoprecipitates.
A controlled, stepwise processing treatment can generate coherent nanoprecipitates in a tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than the untreated alloy at about 800 °C.
The treated alloy will have greater tensile ductility than the untreated alloy at high temperature.
The treated alloy will exhibit delayed crack formation relative to the untreated alloy at high temperature.
The baseline alloy can be characterized as a homogeneous microstructure containing random or incoherent secondary phases, if any.
The proposed mechanism should apply broadly to tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys when nanoprecipitate coherence is maintained.
Alloys with non-coherent or uncontrolled precipitates may respond differently.
The magnitude of ductility and toughness improvement may vary with nanoprecipitate size, volume fraction, and inter-particle spacing.
Long-term stability of coherent interfaces during cyclic high-temperature exposure has not been validated.
Comparing identical alloy compositions under identical tensile-test conditions while varying the nanoprecipitation treatment is intended to isolate the effect of the targeted microstructure.
